1.note: Isaiah is using the word **Woe** to express a strong feeling of warning and judgment against those who seek help from Egypt instead of from Yahweh. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How horrible it will be for]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [so that Egypt will help them]

1.q: עַל־סוּסִ֖ים יִשָּׁעֵ֑נוּ וַ⁠יִּבְטְח֨וּ עַל־רֶ֜כֶב כִּ֣י רָ֗ב וְ⁠עַ֤ל פָּֽרָשִׁים֙ כִּֽי־עָצְמ֣וּ מְאֹ֔ד
1.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [They rely on horses and trust in chariots that are many, indeed, in horsemen that are very numerous]

1.q: וְ⁠לֹ֤א שָׁעוּ֙ עַל־קְד֣וֹשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה לֹ֥א דָרָֽשׁוּ
1.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [but they do not seek help from Yahweh, yes, the Holy One of Israel]

2.note: Isaiah uses the word **Yet** here to indicate a contrast between the wisdom of the Egyptians, in which the people trust, and the wisdom of Yahweh, who will act against them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh is also wise]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **harm**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [disaster on them]

Isaiah is using **he will arise against** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he will take action against.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will take action against]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the evildoers were a **house**, that is, a household or group living together. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the group of evildoers]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those who help]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [evil things]

3.note: Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [is merely human]

Here, **hand** represents the power and capability of Yahweh to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will use his power]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [and the helper and the helped will both go down in defeat]

4.q: כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֣ר יֶהְגֶּה֩ הָ⁠אַרְיֵ֨ה וְ⁠הַ⁠כְּפִ֜יר עַל טַרְפּ֗⁠וֹ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִקָּרֵ֤א עָלָי⁠ו֙ מְלֹ֣א רֹעִ֔ים מִ⁠קּוֹלָ⁠ם֙ לֹ֣א יֵחָ֔ת וּ⁠מֵֽ⁠הֲמוֹנָ֖⁠ם לֹ֣א יַֽעֲנֶ֑ה
4.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion** is undaunted by the shouts of the **shepherds** who come against it and it refuses to abandon its prey, so **Yahweh of Armies** will not be deterred from coming down to fight on **Mount Zion**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [As a lion that growls over its prey cannot be frightened away by the shepherds who gather against it, no matter how much they yell and make noise]

The terms **a lion** and **a young lion** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a mighty lion growls]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fullness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a large number of]

The expression **is called out against it** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [gathers against it]

The expression **it is not frightened by their voice** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [their voice does not frighten it]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [or a young lion growls]

5.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **birds flying** over their nests protect their young, so **Yahweh of Armies** will protectively **cover over Jerusalem**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Like birds hovering over their young to protect them]

6.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if the rebellion of the Israelites were something physically **deep**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have rebelled so severely]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rebellion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [turning away]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if the people of Israel were literally the **sons** of their ancestor Israel. He means the descendants or people of Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of Israel]

7.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [The reason is that]
To translate the phrase **in that day** here and in the rest of this chapter, see how you translated it in [4:1](ta:04). Alternate translation: [at that time]

Here the masculine term **a man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [each person]

The phrase **a man** clarifies how the plural subject **they** will carry out the action: each individual person will reject his own idols. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [each one will reject the idols of his silver]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **idols** that are made of **silver** and **gold**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the idols made from his silver and the idols made from his gold]

The expressions **the idols of his silver** and **the idols of his gold** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the idols made of silver and gold]

In this verse, Isaiah shifts from speaking about the Israelites in the third person (**they** will reject) to addressing them directly in the second person (**your** hands have made for **yourselves**). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a consistent person throughout. Alternate translation: [which their hands have made for themselves]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by sinning]

8.q: וְ⁠נָפַ֤ל אַשּׁוּר֙ בְּ⁠חֶ֣רֶב לֹא־אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠חֶ֥רֶב לֹֽא־אָדָ֖ם תֹּֽאכֲלֶ֑⁠נּוּ
8.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh, not a human army, will destroy the Assyrians]

8.q: בְּ⁠חֶ֣רֶב לֹא אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠חֶ֥רֶב לֹֽא אָדָ֖ם
8.note: Here, **a sword** represents military power and warfare. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by military power not of man, and military power not of mankind]

Isaiah is speaking of **a sword** as if it were a living thing that could **devour** someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a sword not of mankind will kill him]

Here the masculine terms **man** and **mankind** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [humans … humans]

Isaiah is using **from the face of the sword** as a common expression of the culture to mean “away from warfare.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the fighting]

9.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if the Assyrian king or stronghold were a **rock**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And his strong leader will flee in terror]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **terror**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from what terrifies him]

The phrase **the declaration of Yahweh** closes the direct quotation that began in verse 4. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating the end of a direct quotation in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly.

9.q: אֲשֶׁר א֥וּר ל⁠וֹ֙ בְּ⁠צִיּ֔וֹן וְ⁠תַנּ֥וּר ל֖⁠וֹ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
9.note: Here Isaiah is speaking as if Yahweh’s judgment and power were a **fire** and a **furnace** in Jerusalem. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whose power to destroy is in Zion and whose burning judgment is in Jerusalem]
